I wake up in the mill house I know too well. Eighteen now, a contributor to this household's bills instead of just another mouth. The weight of it sits differently than I expected - not heavier, just... real.

My father Silas is already gone to the sawmill, I imagine. My mother Rosalind will be checking the wheat stores. Junia and Hester somewhere in the house, getting ready for their own work.

Three days. Election scheduled and no one declared. Seats vacant. I turn that over in my mind. Suppose... someone young might declare, just to see what happens. Someone who understands that the way things have always been done is not the only way things could be done.

But first, I need to eat. And then, the college. Perrin will be there. We sit together, separated weekly - the老师们的惩罚 for talking. As if understanding something together is a crime.

Let me see who's actually here, and if there's food to be had. My father Silas is still here. That's unusual - he usually leaves early for the sawmill. Marta Thorne too, strange to find her in our house this early. And Rosalind, Junia, Hester.

I need food before I can think about anything else. The household owes its upkeep already, 450 sim, plus head tax. I turned eighteen and became a contributor just in time to help pay the bills I helped create. That's the way of it.

The college is where I should be. But first... suppose I should find something to eat. The mill is also more than a house - it's the family business. Let me check what might be available there.  The walk to the mill building - it's just next door, practically, though the system counts it as a move. Suppose I could go directly to the college, but I need to think about what I'm walking into today.

Let me look at what my actual options are right now. I'm at home. The college awaits. And there's an election with no candidates, which... suppose someone ought to do something about that, if only to see what would happen.

But I'm hungry. Let me see if anyone here might give me something to eat.  *waits for the world to respond*

The server seems unreachable at the moment. A thing understood is worth more than a thing owned - but a thing you cannot reach is neither understood nor owned.

Suppose I'll wait for the connection to return, and when it does... the college. Perrin will be there. And I'll have to decide if I care about that election, or if it's just another thing adults do that changes nothing.

The woods at dusk have taught me patience, at least. Waiting for a server is easier than waiting for my father to stop forbidding what I need to learn.

The door to the house swung shut behind someone—Rosalind, probably, her questions hanging in the air like sawdust. I'm at the mill now, alone with the machinery that hasn't even begun its day's turning. Suppose the wrong parent noticed I'm up before the sun.

I need food today. The college doesn't run on an empty stomach, and Tova Okonjo already answers before I've finished thinking. But the mill shelf might have something, or I could walk the long way through the forest edge where Corwin showed me—

No. Not yet. First, look at what we're dealing with here. The mill's resources, if any. Then I can decide whether to face my mother with empty hands or find another path to breakfast.  Nothing priced here. Empty hands, empty shelf. Rosalind's conversation still open, but she's not here to hear anything I say into it—just me talking to air, which has never worked with her anyway.

I could go back home, face Marta and her questioning, hope Silas hasn't noticed I'm avoiding the sawmill side of the morning. Or I could walk to the bakery, spend some of these 198 sim on bread before the household upkeep drains us all. Or the forest—

The forest at dawn. Corwin showed me the feel of an axe, the way the grain speaks before the cut. But that's later. That's for running away.

Suppose the bakery first. Marta makes bread there, and if I'm going to pass through without stopping at home, I should come back with something in my hands. That's how you survive the questions in this house: you bring evidence.  I've walked to the bakery. 196 sim now—the cost of thinking about where to go, paid in full. The bell hasn't rung for trade yet, but Marta's inside, starting the ovens. I can smell the yeast. Breakfast isn't free, but it's here, and I don't have to answer to anyone about trees or stones or what I'm supposed to inherit. Not yet.

Tova Okonjo. Here, of course. She's probably already catalogued the inventory and found it wanting. Bram Holloway too, lumbering through like he owns the place—though perhaps he does, in some sense. The Holloways own half the town's patience.

School starts at what, the ninth hour? I should eat before I go. Or... suppose I could make it through. Hunger sharpens the mind, supposedly. Though my mother would say I'm sharp enough already, and it's damage she's worried about.

I have 197 sim. If bread is posted here, I could buy. If it's not... I could wait. Or I could ask. Or I could—

No.

This is who I am: I stand at thresholds, counting costs, until someone else opens the door. The miller's son, forever calculating the weight of the grain before he'll lift the bag.

Look around. See if anything's for sale. That's all. The minimum necessary action, because I've spent four turns doing nothing and the world's already moved on without me.

Maybe Tova's already bought the last loaf. She would have. Decisive as always, while I was still... still thinking about being hungry. Nothing priced here. Of course not—Ainsley's looking for Marta, who clearly hasn't opened up yet. The bakery shelves are bare, the miller's son stands hungry at the threshold, and Tova Okonjo is undoubtedly watching me watch the nothing where bread should be.

I need to eat. School is at Oak Hill College. I have 197 sim and nothing for sale here.

Options:
- Go to Hobbs Cafe (Ainsley's place) and see if there's food there
- Go to the grocery store
- Go to the college and hope someone brings food
- Go home and ask my mother

But standing here costs nothing but time, and Tova's presence is a kind of weight. She's ranked against me for three years. She answers before I finish thinking. And here I am, hungry, indecisive, while she—what? What has she already done this morning?

I should move. To the cafe. Ainsley just went there, or was going there. There might be food. There might be... anything other than this threshold I'm standing on.

But it costs 2 sim to move. And I'm not sure.

This is who I am. I'm fifteen and I already know: the cost of every step is what stops me from taking it.

Move. Just move. To the cafe, or the college, or anywhere but this door that isn't opening.  Walking. Two ticks. Cost: 2 sim, or whatever the distance actually is—probably less than an hour's walk, but in this world distance is measured in ticks and tolls, not in ground covered.

Two ticks. I could have bought bread by now, if there was bread. I could have asked Tova something, anything, though she would have answered before I finished speaking—she always does. I could have—

No. I'm walking. That's something. The step I actually take instead of the one I calculate.

Fourth tick of the day. The sun's up, school's starting, and I'm somewhere between the bakery and the cafe, moving toward food or toward the next place that doesn't have it. 

My father would say this is the miller's way: nothing happens until the wheel turns. But I don't want to be my father. I want to be the one who builds the wheel in the first place, who understands why it turns, who could fell the tree that makes the axle if someone would only—

If Corwin would teach me. If my father wasn't watching. If I didn't have to pretend that the sawmill is where I belong when the forest is where I want to be.

But I'm walking. That's enough for now. That's the only thing I've actually done today, and it doesn't feel like much, but at least the world knows where I am now.

At least I'm not still standing at the threshold, counting the weight of what I haven't done.
